metadata.source: Dravyaguna Vijñāna (Dravya_guna3_med_p2.pdf) — Appendix: Therapeutic (Disease-Wise) Indication of Drugs
metadata.notes: Continuation batch 2. Covers F–L diseases. Botanical names cross-referenced with standard Ayurvedic pharmacognosy.

diseases.description: Elevated body temperature as a systemic response to infection or inflammation. Ayurveda describes jvara as the king of diseases — it is the first disorder to afflict a being and the last to leave. Eight types are described based on doṣa involvement, with unique presentations and management protocols for each.
Fever accompanied by intense burning sensation in the body, palms, soles, and eyes. A pitta-dominant type of jvara. Requires cooling, pitta-pacifying, and antipyretic therapy simultaneously.

Parasitic infection by filarial worms causing lymphatic obstruction, swelling of limbs (elephantiasis), and scrotal enlargement. In Ayurveda ślīpada is caused by vitiated kapha, vāta, and rakta with parasitic organisms obstructing the lymphatic channels.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: An abnormal tunnel or tract from the anal canal to the skin near the anus, typically resulting from an abscess. In Ayurveda bhagandara is caused by vitiated tridoṣa, typically beginning as an abscess (vidradhi) in the anal region. Requires kṣāra karma (caustic treatment) or surgery in classical texts.

herbs.name: Nyagrodhādigaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group of five fig trees (Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Asvattha, Plaksha, Madhuka)

diseases.description: Distension of the abdomen by accumulated gas in the intestines, causing discomfort, bloating, and audible rumbling. In Ayurveda, a vāta disorder caused by impaired digestive fire and gas accumulation in the pakvāśaya.
Foul-smelling ear discharge indicating chronic infection (otitis media with perforation) or cholesteatoma. In Ayurveda linked to kapha accumulation and kṛmi (microbial) involvement in the ear canal.
Intrauterine growth restriction or atrophy of the foetus. In Ayurveda indicates deficiency of nutritive rasa and depletion of stanya (nutritive maternal fluids) reaching the foetus.

Abnormal body odour — not just sweat odour but deep systemic malodour arising from metabolic imbalance, āma accumulation, or skin conditions. In Ayurveda related to vitiated pitta, rakta, and accumulation of kleda (body waste).

Breaking of a bone due to trauma, stress, or pathological weakness. In Ayurveda the healing of bones (asthi dhātu) is supported by herbs that promote sandhi (union), strengthen the bone tissue, and reduce vāta which governs the skeletal system.

Medicated smoke therapy (dhūmapāna) used for respiratory conditions, neurological diseases, and rituals. Also used as disinfectant fumigation for rooms, wounds, and body cavities. A specialised Ayurvedic treatment modality.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Useful to disorders caused by bhūtas (evil spirits or micro-organisms)

diseases.description: Herbs that promote milk secretion in nursing mothers. Insufficient lactation is a common post-partum concern. In Ayurveda linked to depletion of rasa dhātu and kapha, which form the nutritive basis of breast milk.

Herbs that purify breast milk when it becomes vitiated — causing the nursing infant to suffer from colic, skin problems, or fever. Maternal dietary or disease factors can vitiate stanya (breast milk) according to Ayurveda.

herbs.name: Jīvakādyagaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group of eight vitalising herbs (Jivaka, Rsabhaka, etc.)

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

diseases.description: Inflammation and enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck forming a chain-like swelling. Often indicates tuberculosis of lymph nodes (scrofula) or other infections. Ayurveda considers it a kapha-dominant disease with involvement of meda dhātu.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Reducing body weight; cutting unctuous materials

diseases.description: Abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland causing a visible swelling at the front of the neck. In Ayurveda, galagaṇḍa is a kapha-medas condition involving the gala (throat) region. Can be associated with hypothyroidism.

herbs.name: Śālasārādigaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group including Sal and related trees

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Sexually transmitted bacterial infection causing painful urination, purulent urethral or vaginal discharge. In Ayurveda classified under mūtrakṛcchra and the prameha group. Involves vitiated pitta, rakta, and śukra dhātu.

Chronic digestive disorder involving impaired digestion, irregular bowel habits alternating between constipation and diarrhoea, malabsorption, and nutritional deficiency. Involves the grahaṇī (small intestine, site of digestive fire) and is one of the eight major diseases in classical Ayurveda.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Checking frequency and liquidity of stool; anti-diarrhoeal

diseases.description: A severe type of spreading skin infection characterised by glandular nodular swellings combined with erysipelas-like spread. A complex condition involving rakta, māṁsa, and meda dhātu vitiation.

Small sand-like or gravel-like particles in urine, preceding or accompanying kidney stone formation. In Ayurveda indicates early crystallisation in the mūtravaha srotas. Treated with diuretics and lithotriptic herbs.
Premature or pathological greying of hair. In Ayurveda caused by excess pitta, mental stress, improper diet, and genetic factors. Differentiated from natural ageing-related greying.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Causing greying of hairs (herbs to avoid)

diseases.description: Infestation by the guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis) causing painful blistering and a long worm emerging through the skin. In Ayurveda classified as a type of kṛmiroga (worm disease) involving deep tissue parasites.

Abdominal masses, cysts, and tumour-like growths in the abdomen — including uterine fibroids, mesenteric cysts, and bowel-related masses. One of the eight major diseases in Ayurveda. Five types: vātaja, pittaja, kaphaja, raktaja, and sannipātaja.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Breaking faecal mass or abdominal lump; Incision (surgical process)

diseases.description: A type of gulma (abdominal mass) specifically involving vitiated rakta (blood) — can present as uterine or intestinal haematoma or blood clot formation in the abdominal cavity. A severe and difficult-to-treat condition.

Blood in the urine — can be visible (gross haematuria) or microscopic. Indicates urinary tract infection, kidney stone, injury, or tumour. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and rakta affecting the mūtravaha srotas.

herbs.name: Parṇiṇī-catuṣṭya
herbs.botanical: Group of four leafy herbs (Salaparni, Prsniparni, Masaparni, Mudgaparni)

diseases.description: Abnormal external or internal bleeding from blood vessels. In Ayurveda caused by excess pitta vitiating the rakta dhātu, leading to raktapitta (intrinsic haemorrhage) or external bleeding from wounds and orifices.

A severe, advanced form of jaundice with extreme pallor, weakness, and systemic biliousness. In Ayurveda described as a critical stage where all three doṣas are involved, affecting the liver and rasa dhātu profoundly.

General category for diseases of the head including headache, migraine, scalp disorders, and cerebral conditions. In Ayurveda the head (śiras) is considered the most vital body part — seat of prāṇa, the ten sensory organs, and the mind.

herbs.name: Mahat pan
herbs.botanical: Cyclea peltata (Lam.) Hook. f. & Thoms. (large leaf)

diseases.description: Therapeutic procedure to evacuate accumulated doṣas from the head region — includes nasal drops (nasya) and herbal inhalations. Used for chronic sinusitis, migraine, neurological conditions, and general head-cleansing as part of Panchakarma.

Pain in the head region — primary (migraine, tension, cluster) or secondary. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta, pitta, kapha, or tridoṣa in the śiras. Includes different types like ardhāvabhedaka (hemicranial), sūryāvartta (solar), and ānantavāta.

Diseases of the heart including heart failure, coronary artery disease, valvular disorders, and arrhythmias. In Ayurveda the hṛdaya is the seat of consciousness (ojas), prāṇa, and all dhātus. Hṛdroga has five types: vataja, pittaja, kaphaja, tridoṣaja, and kṛmija.

Protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weak spot in the muscle or connective tissue wall. In Ayurveda āntravṛddhi (inguinal hernia) involves prolapse of intestinal loops through the abdominal wall, caused by vitiated vāta.

Involuntary contractions of the diaphragm causing characteristic sounds. In Ayurveda, hikkā is a vāta-pitta disorder involving upward movement of prāṇa vāta through the respiratory and gastrointestinal passages. Five types are described — some considered life-threatening.

Rough, breathy, or strained voice quality due to inflammation or dysfunction of the larynx and vocal cords. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta and kapha in the kaṇṭha (throat) region, overuse of voice, or respiratory infections.

Involuntary leakage of urine. In Ayurveda, a vāta disorder of the mūtravaha srotas causing loss of sphincter control. Can occur in elderly patients, post-partum women, or due to neurological conditions.

General impaired digestion — food not being properly digested, causing discomfort, fullness, nausea, and belching. Differentiated in Ayurveda into āmājīrṇa (ama-type), vidagdhājīrṇa (acid-type), viṣṭabdhājīrṇa (constipation-type), and rasaśeṣājīrṇa (residual type).

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Promoting desire for food and relish
Causing loss of digestive power (for excess agni types)

diseases.description: Indigestion characterised by undigested food accumulating as āma — causing heaviness, nausea, white coating on the tongue, and systemic toxicity. The most fundamental type of indigestion leading to all āma-related diseases.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Digestant for mala (āma) or faeces (associated with āma)
Digestive for food (annapācana); digestive for āmadoṣa (āmadoṣapācana)

diseases.description: Inability to properly digest ghee (clarified butter) — causing heaviness, nausea, and oiliness. A specific type of indigestion relevant to Ayurvedic treatments involving sneha (oleation therapy), where too much ghee causes lipid overload.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating complications of the intake of ghṛta (unacting material) including hyperlipidaemia

diseases.description: Swelling and inflammation of tissues — can be local or systemic. In Ayurveda, śotha (oedema/inflammation) is caused by vitiated vāta, pitta, kapha, or all three doṣas. Includes joint inflammation, soft tissue swelling, and systemic inflammatory conditions.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Eliminating impurities and thereby making the body pure and healthy

diseases.description: Swelling and inflammation of the lips — can result from infection, allergy, vitamin deficiency, or trauma. In Ayurveda a pitta-kapha condition of the mukha region.

Mental derangement, psychosis, or severe psychiatric disorder. In Ayurveda unmāda is caused by vitiated doṣas affecting the hṛdaya (seat of consciousness). Six types are described: vātaja, pittaja, kaphaja, tridoṣaja, and two exogenous types (due to grief and supernatural causes).

Inability to fall asleep or stay asleep, leading to daytime fatigue and cognitive impairment. In Ayurveda insomnia is primarily a vāta disorder, with pitta involvement causing an overactive mind. Disturbed prāṇa vāta and tarpaka kapha are key.

Bleeding from multiple orifices (nose, mouth, ear, anus, urethra) caused by vitiated pitta reaching the rakta dhātu. One of the most serious conditions in classical Ayurveda, involving five types based on direction of bleeding. Analogous to haemorrhagic disorders, coagulopathy, and vitamin deficiency bleeding.

Yellowish discolouration of the skin, sclera, and mucous membranes due to elevated bilirubin. In Ayurveda, kāmalā is caused by vitiated pitta and rakta affecting the liver (yakṛt). Three types described: śakha kāmalā, kumbha kāmalā, and halimaka (most severe).
Toxicity from date palm (Kharjūra) or related substances. In classical Ayurveda, various plant-derived toxins were classified and specific antidotes prescribed.
Stretch marks during or after pregnancy. In Ayurveda caused by rapid distension of skin tissue during pregnancy affecting the māṁsa and tvak (skin) dhātus.
Muscle cramps — sudden, painful, involuntary muscle contractions. In Ayurveda a vāta disorder affecting the māṁsa (muscle) and sira (vessels) causing spasm.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Pacifying vāta heated in dhātus and skin

diseases.description: Parasitic or microbial infestation in the ear canal causing itching, discharge, and pain. In Ayurveda classified as a kṛmi (parasitic organism) disease affecting the karṇa, requiring antimicrobial ear drops.

A type of chronic arthritis specifically affecting one knee joint with distinctive swelling resembling the head of a jackal (kroṣṭu). Caused by accumulated vāta and kapha in the knee joint, resulting in persistent swelling, stiffness, and pain.

Wasting disease secondary to chest wound or injury — characterised by haemoptysis, emaciation, and progressive debility. An injury-induced consumption closely related to kṣayaja kāsa (cough of depletion). Requires nourishing, haemostatic, and wound-healing therapy.

herbs.name: Jīvakādyagaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group of eight vitalising herbs (Jivaka, Rsabhaka etc.)

diseases.description: The classical Ayurvedic category of severe chronic skin diseases — ranging from leprosy (Hansen's disease) to severe psoriasis, dermatitis, and ichthyosis. Kuṣṭha is of two types: mahā kuṣṭha (seven major types) and kṣudra kuṣṭha (eleven minor types). Caused by vitiated tridoṣa affecting the seven dhātus of the skin.

herbs.name: Pañcatikta
herbs.botanical: Group of five bitter herbs (Nimba, Patola, Guduchi, Vasa, Kantakari)

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Anti-leprosy/skin disease; destroying severe skin diseases

diseases.description: Abnormal white or yellowish vaginal discharge. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated kapha and vāta affecting the yonimārga (vaginal tract). Can result from infection, hormonal imbalance, or cervical pathology.

Hepatomegaly — enlargement of the liver beyond its normal size. Can result from infections (viral hepatitis), fatty liver, cirrhosis, or haematological conditions. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and kapha obstructing the yakṛt (liver).
Trismus — inability to open the mouth due to spasm of the jaw muscles. In Ayurveda a vāta-dominant condition involving the hanu (jaw) region. Can be caused by tetanus, dental infection, or trauma.

Intermittent fever with cyclical chills, rigors, sweating, and systemic symptoms caused by Plasmodium parasites. In Ayurveda classified as viṣamajvara — irregular fever — with three types: anyedyuṣka (tertian), tṛtīyaka (quartan), and cāturthaka (quartan). Caused by external pathogenic factors (āgantu) in addition to doṣa vitiation.

Inflammation or infection of the breast tissue, most commonly in breastfeeding women. Causes pain, redness, swelling, and fever. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and kapha obstructing the stanya-vaha srotas.

Herbal preparations specifically enhancing intellect, memory, concentration, and cognitive function. Medhya rasāyana is a special subset of rasāyana (rejuvenation) therapy targeting the mind and nervous system. Charaka describes four specific medhya rasāyana herbs.

Excessive, prolonged, or irregular uterine bleeding. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and rakta affecting the ārtava (menstrual blood) and uterus. One of the most common gynaecological conditions treated in classical Ayurveda.

General category of psychiatric and psychological disorders. In Ayurveda includes anxiety, depression, psychosis, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive tendencies. Caused by vitiation of the three psychological qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) and imbalance of doṣas affecting the manas.

Tissue death and gangrene — loss of sensation and progressive death of body tissues. In Ayurveda related to severe vāta obstruction causing loss of prāṇa in tissues. Requires rasāyana, bṛṁhaṇa, and wound-healing therapies.

Non-cancerous growth in the nasal cavity or sinuses causing nasal obstruction, loss of smell, and chronic congestion. In Ayurveda caused by kapha accumulation in the nāsā region forming a māṁsa-piṇḍa (tissue mass).

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Inability or difficulty seeing in dim light or darkness. Caused by vitamin A deficiency or retinal degeneration. In Ayurveda classified as a vāta-pitta condition affecting the śalāka (rod cells) of the retina, with deficiency of rasa dhātu reaching the eye.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Promoting body-weight; nourishing (rasa dhātu for eye nutrition)
